messages.author: ef76f4ec1ca10943
messages.subject: spatial effect fit in co-distribution models
parts:
Dear INLA team,

I am interested in fitting a semi-continuous model similar to the one in the spde-tutorial by Elias. Everything is greatly explained by the way. I would like to adjust a common spatial random effect for the binomial and the continuous models in order to take into account the non-presence in the spatial effect of the continuous part (which is the most important in my case). Said all this, I have one major question about the co-distribution when applying the "copy model" command:

- when I copy a spde model with fixed=TRUE inside the f() command, the spatial effect is fitted using the first dataset/likelihood, or is it co-fitted with the second dataset/likelihood?

I mean, for example: ("1" is binomial , "2" is continuous)

    formula <- Y ~ 0 + intercept1 + intercept2 + f(spatial1, model=spde) + f(spatial2, copy="spatial1",fixed=T)


In this case, the effect is fitted only using spatial1? or both spatial1 and spatial2 jointly?

If it is not the second, is there any way of doing it??

many thanks in advance.
Iosu

the copy just makes internally an almost identical copy of the model,
the indexing is just differently.

so

f(spatial1,model=spde)+f(spatial2,copy="spatial1")

do this in pratice, using index'es spatial2 for the second term. the
second f() refer to the same model and realisation of the first f(),
just that the indexing is different.


so I think it do what you want it to do

On 20/08/13 14:36, paradin...@gmail.com wrote:
> the copy just makes internally an almost identical copy of the model,
> the indexing is just differently.
>
> so
>
> f(spatial1,model=spde)+f(spatial2,copy="spatial1")
>
> do this in pratice, using index'es spatial2 for the second term. the
> second f() refer to the same model and realisation of the first f(),
> just that the indexing is different.
>
>
> mmmm, but the second f() refers to the same model of the first, which is
> fitted with the first dataset, right? not taking into account both.
>
> basically, the reason for this question is that generally what we
> "biologists" do, is fit the spatial effect using densities > 0 and
> forget the rest. And I understand that we can be loosing valuable
> information coming from the non-presence.

If you construct the model so that all the datasets are there, all
effect estimates will use the joint information; the "copy" should be
seen as just an internal technicality, and it truly is the same field in
both parts of the model.
Schematically,
y1 = p1(f(x1))
y2 = p2(f(x2))
x = x1 = x2

One can either estimate the two models separately, and not require
x1=x2, yielding two different x estimates, or specify both models with
the requirement x=x1=x2 in the same inla formula using "copy", in which
case both y1 and y2 will influence the estimate of x.
I _think_ that's essentially what your question is about...

Finn

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial effect fit in co-distribution models
parts:
> mmmm, but the second f() refers to the same model of the first, which
> is fitted with the first dataset, right? not taking into account both

No. It's a trick to make possible to put a same random
effect on the linear predictor for each likelihood.
So, the information from both dataset is used.
Setting fixed=TRUE (for the copy) you just says that the
random effect entry with same variance on 'both' linear predictor.

A simplest example:

n <- 500
x <- arima.sim(n=n, model=list(ar=0.7))
y1 <- x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.02)
y2 <- x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

Y <- cbind(c(y1, rep(NA,n)), c(rep(NA,n), y2))

require(INLA)
r <- inla(resp ~ f(i, model='ar1') + f(j, copy='i'),
data=list(resp=Y, i=c(1:n, rep(NA,n)), j=c(rep(NA,n), 1:n)),
family=rep('gaussian',2))
r$summary.hy

The copy feature implies not an exact copy but a copy with a tiny noise.
the precision of this noise is

f(i2,copy="i1", precision=1e9)

which is the default. this is so that the joint distribution is
non-singular.

you may try to reduce this number (or increase it), to see if that makes
a difference.

I would not expect that summary numbers like DIC/WAIC will match for
every digit...

H

parts:
this is true. fixed=TRUE is default, however, so unless you say
fixed=FALSE, then this should not be the problem.

Ok, I see.

Yes in my case, since both predictors are in a different scale (presence/absence & abundance), so I had to specify fixed=F.

However I thought that the scaling parameter would be Z in one model and 1/Z in the other. Isn´t it? In such case, shouldn´t the fit of both models be *equal*?

No, only the copy has the extra parameter. Think of the case where you have more than one extra copy; then the reciprocal construction you describe wouldn't be possible.

It is however possible to symmetries this by precisely doing that; make _two_ copies, and have all NA in the original f().
f(dummy, ...) + f(i1, copy="dummy", fixed=FALSE) + f(i2, copy="dummy",fixed=FALSE)
Where dummy=rep(NA, n) and you need to specify some more parameters to that f() to tell inla how big the model should be etc.
In this case the "dummy" model has an unidentifiable scaling parameter, so you would want to fixed that parameter to avoid overparameterisation.
(I know of one person who have used this approach successfully.)

Finn

yes, this is likely the issue. since the prior is defined for the
scaling, beta, where you have

z1
z2 = beta*z1

or you have

z2
z1 = z2/beta


since the prior for beta and 1/beta is not the same, it will give
different marginal likelihood, DIC++

hyper=list(theta=list(initial=0, fixed=TRUE))) +
f(i, copy="i0", fixed=FALSE) +
f(j, copy="i0", fixed=FALSE) +
f(k, copy="i0", fixed=FALSE) +
f(l, copy="i0", fixed=FALSE)

rrrr = inla(formula, data = data.frame(y, i, j, k, l, i0, w0),
control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE))

cbind(diff.dic = r$dic$dic-rrrr$dic$dic,
diff.waic = r$waic$waic-rrrr$waic$waic,
diff.ml = r$ml[1]-rrrr$ml[2]) ### reasonable difference...


### Beta's values are repective to marginal variance = 1, as next plot shows
rrrr$summary.hyperpar
plot(rrrr)

plot(r$summary.fitted.val$mean, rrrr$summary.fitted.val$mean);
abline(0:1,col=0,lwd=5,lty=3)
